content:
I became unbearable so gradually that I almost missed it.

At first, I was simply busy.

The council was preparing a new housing survey. The eastern clinic needed supply allocations. Toph’s academy wanted permits for an expanded training yard. Aang’s Air Nomad school had acquired land but no legal category because Cranefish Town had never needed a form for “religious-cultural educational sanctuary with large flying mammals.”

I created one.

That should have warned me.

Instead I started waking before the others so I could work in the quiet room at the back of the house.

Then I began bringing papers to breakfast.

Then dinner.

Then bed, once, until Katara removed them from my lap and said, “Absolutely not.”

“I’m almost done.”

“No.”

“It’s one page.”

“No.”

“Half a page.”

Toph, already under the blankets, said, “I support Sugar Queen’s dictatorship.”

I laughed.

I put the papers away.

Then I waited until everyone slept and got them back out.

Three nights later, I snapped at Aang for humming.

He stopped immediately.

The silence that followed was worse than the humming had been.

“I’m sorry,” I said.

“It’s okay.”

It was not.

The next morning I apologized again by making tea.

The morning after that, I forgot I had agreed to meet Katara for lunch.

She waited forty minutes.

When I finally arrived at the clinic, breathless and carrying three folders, she was sitting on the steps with two untouched bowls beside her.

“Oh.”

The sound came out small.

Katara looked at me.

She did not yell.

That was worse too.

“I’m sorry.”

“I know.”

“I lost track of time.”

“I know.”

“I can still—”

“No.”

Her voice was gentle.

Firm.

I stopped.

Katara stood and handed one bowl to a passing medic.

“Come home when you’re done.”

Then she went back inside.

I spent the afternoon furious.

Not at her.

That would have been easier.

At myself for disappointing her. At the council for needing everything. At the city for growing problems faster than we could solve them. At every person who had told me I was useful until usefulness became the closest thing I had to proof that I deserved to stay.

I worked later.

Of course I did.

When I got home, the house was quiet.

Toph sat at the kitchen table.

She did not look up.

“You’re lying.”

I put down my bag. “I haven’t said anything.”

“Your whole body is lying.”

“That’s not how—”

“Don’t explain seismic sense to me, Paperwork.”

I shut my mouth.

Toph tapped one finger against the table.

“You walk different when you’re hiding something.”

“I’m tired.”

“Yeah.”

“That’s it.”

“No.”

I hated how quickly the word landed.

“Where are Aang and Katara?”

“Roof.”

“Why?”

“Because Katara wanted to yell at you and Aang told her to wait until you ate.”

My stomach dropped.

Toph’s mouth twitched.

“That was a joke.”

“Not funny.”

“Little funny.”

She pushed a bowl toward me.

I sat.

The food was warm.

That meant somebody had reheated it recently.

My throat tightened for reasons that made me angry.

“I’m fine.”

Toph’s expression hardened.

“Do you think I’m stupid?”

“No.”

“Then stop giving me stupid answers.”

There it was.

No gentle invitation. No careful opening.

Toph had spent her childhood trapped behind people deciding what she could handle. She considered dishonesty a kind of locked door.

I stared at the soup.

“If I stop,” I said, “things fall through.”

“Some things.”

“Important things.”

“Sure.”

“People could get hurt.”

Toph leaned back.

“And if you don’t stop?”

I did not answer.

She listened to my silence.

“People still get hurt,” she said.

That was cruel.

It was also accurate.

Katara had waited with two bowls.

Aang had stopped humming because my nerves had turned his joy into noise.

Toph had been sitting alone in the kitchen waiting for my footsteps.

I rubbed both hands over my face.

“I don’t know how to be needed a normal amount.”

The confession escaped before I could stop it.

Toph went quiet.

Then she stood.

For one awful second I thought she was leaving.

Instead she came around the table and sat on the floor beside my chair, back against my shin.

Not looking at me.

Not making me look at her.

“Yeah,” she said.

One word.

Understanding without pretending we had the same wound.

I ate the soup.

When the bowl was empty, Toph shouted, “You can come down now!”

Aang’s voice answered from the roof. “We weren’t listening!”

“You’re a terrible liar!”

Katara came downstairs first.

Her anger was still there.

Good.

I did not want it erased because I finally admitted I was struggling.

She sat across from me.

“I was hurt.”

“I know.”

“Don’t say it like that ends the sentence.”

I swallowed.

“I was hurt that you forgot me. And I’m scared because you’re treating exhaustion like evidence you’re doing enough.”

Aang sat beside her.

I looked at the three of them.

“I’m sorry.”

Katara nodded once. “Thank you.”

I waited for forgiveness.

She did not hand it over immediately.

That was another thing I loved about her. Katara believed in compassion, but she did not confuse compassion with pretending harm had not happened.

“What do you need?” Aang asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That can be true,” he said. “But it can’t be the end of the conversation forever.”

Toph tilted her head back against my knee. “Look at Twinkle Toes growing a spine.”

“I’ve had one.”

“You borrowed mine.”

Katara almost smiled.

I looked toward the hallway leading to my office.

The door was open.

Papers covered the desk.

For weeks I had treated that room as proof I had boundaries while carrying work out of it constantly.

“I need the door rule back,” I said.

Katara frowned. “The door rule?”

“When I leave that room, work stays there unless there’s an actual emergency.”

Toph raised a hand. “Define emergency.”

“Fire. Flood. Building collapse. Active violence. Somebody will lose food, shelter, medicine, or legal protection before morning if I do nothing.”

“No flags?” Aang asked.

“No flags.”

“Even ugly ones?”

“Especially ugly ones.”

Toph nodded solemnly. “Brave.”

Katara said, “One day off each week.”

I opened my mouth.

She stared at me.

“One day,” I agreed.

Aang added, “And if you miss plans, you tell the person why before you start apologizing. Not so we can excuse it. So you don’t hide behind ‘busy.’”

That one hurt.

Which meant it belonged in the agreement.

I nodded.

Katara’s shoulders lowered slightly.

“I’m still mad.”

“I know.”

“But I don’t want to punish you.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying that.”

“Sorry.”

Toph snorted.

Katara’s mouth betrayed her with the beginning of a smile.

I reached across the table, palm up.

She looked at my hand.

Then took it.

Not everything repaired in one gesture.

The next week, I forgot myself twice.

The first time, Toph walked into my office at dinner and rang Aang’s ceremonial bell beside my ear.

I screamed.

The second time, Katara simply stood in the doorway holding my coat.

I looked at the unfinished report.

Then at her.

I closed the folder.

We walked to a noodle stall three streets away.

Aang met us there after a meeting. Toph arrived ten minutes later with two students and no explanation for why one had blue paint in his hair.

Nobody asked me about the report.

For the first half hour, I kept thinking about it anyway.

Then Aang challenged Toph to balance noodles on chopsticks using only airbending and seismic sense, which was exactly as stupid as it sounded.

Katara laughed into my shoulder.

My body, traitor that it was, began to unclench.

Silence had many shapes.

There was the good kind: four people reading in the same room, the scratch of pen and whisper of turning pages, nobody demanding anything.

There was the sacred kind: Aang meditating, Katara healing, Toph listening to the earth.

And there was the wrong kind.

The silence made when I swallowed every need until the people who loved me had to guess what was happening from the damage around it.

I was trying to learn the difference.

Slowly.

Loudly, according to Toph.

But learning.

The repair began with one rule: I was not allowed to apologize for resting.

This proved harder than resting itself.

Every time I woke from a nap and saw someone else working, guilt climbed into my throat before I could stop it. Katara caught me once halfway through saying sorry and held up one finger.

“No.”

“But—”

“No.”

Toph, from the floor, said, “If you apologize again, I’m charging you.”

Aang looked up from his papers. “Can we actually do that?”

“No,” I said.

“Shame.”

The joke did not cure me.

It gave me enough room to practice.

Eventually, rest stopped feeling like stolen time. Not always. Enough that I could close my eyes without first earning permission from an imaginary judge.

Some nights I still apologized. The difference was that now I heard myself doing it, and sometimes I could stop halfway through.
